title: The King's Dream: A Statue and a Stone
summary: Nebuchadnezzar demands that his experts tell him both his dream and its meaning, and when they cannot, he orders all the wise men killed. Daniel and his friends pray, God reveals the mystery, and Daniel describes a great statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and clay, shattered by a stone cut without human hands that becomes a mountain filling the earth. The king honors Daniel's God and promotes Daniel and his friends.
story: Chapter 1 showed that God gave Daniel insight into visions and dreams; chapter 2 puts that gift to work in a crisis of life and death. It also sets out the book's large picture of history for the first time. The statue's four metals stand for a series of kingdoms, beginning with Nebuchadnezzar's own, and the stone stands for a kingdom that "the God of heaven will set up" and that "will never be destroyed" (verse 44). Chapter 7 will return to the same four kingdoms through beasts rather than metals, and the two chapters frame the Aramaic heart of the book. The story also establishes Daniel and his friends in high office, which sets up the tests to come in chapters 3 and 6.
historical:
The dream comes in Nebuchadnezzar's second year, about 603 BC, early in a reign that lasted until 562 BC. That date sits awkwardly with the three years of training in chapter 1, and interpreters explain it in different ways: by the Babylonian practice of counting the accession year separately, so that the training could span parts of three years, or by supposing the stories were once told separately. Either way, the king is young in power and anxious about the future of what he has built.

The wise men of verse 2 were real classes of Babylonian experts. Babylonian scholars kept long collections of omens, and a whole literature of dream interpretation existed in Mesopotamia, including dream books that listed what a given dream signified. What the king demands is outside that system: they can interpret a dream once it is told, but no manual can tell a man what he dreamed. His suspicion that they would invent a pleasing interpretation (verse 9) was not unreasonable.
cultural:
At verse 4 the text changes language. The astrologers answer the king "in Aramaic", and from that point until the end of chapter 7 the book itself is written in Aramaic, the international language of diplomacy and trade under Babylon and Persia. It may simply mark the switch, the way a modern book might note that a conversation is in French, but it also means that these chapters about God's rule over the nations are written in the nations' own language.

Kings in the ancient Near East took dreams seriously as messages from the gods, and a troubling royal dream could shake a court. Nebuchadnezzar's threat to cut the experts in pieces and turn their houses to rubble reflects the absolute power of a king over his servants. Daniel's response is to seek time, gather his friends, and pray to "the God of heaven" (verse 18), a title for Israel's God common in the Persian period and used in texts written for an international audience. His prayer of praise (verses 20 to 23) is a small psalm: God changes times and seasons, removes and sets up kings, and reveals what is hidden. That is the thesis of the book in a few lines.
literary: The chapter is a court story of a familiar kind: a king faces a problem, his experts fail, a young outsider succeeds by divine help and is rewarded. Daniel insists that the credit is not his (verse 30). The dream itself is built on a descending order, from gold to silver to bronze to iron to iron mixed with clay, lessening in value but, in the case of iron, increasing in hardness and violence. The stone is its opposite: not made by human hands, small at first, and then a mountain filling the whole earth. The chapter uses the word mystery repeatedly, and it ends with the pagan king confessing that Daniel's God is "the God of gods and Lord of kings, the Revealer of Mysteries" (verse 47), a pattern of royal confession that recurs in chapters 3, 4, and 6.

outline.t: The king's dream and his impossible demand
Daniel asks for time, prays, and praises the God who reveals
Daniel before the king: the credit belongs to God
The dream: a statue of four metals and a stone
The interpretation: four kingdoms and God's everlasting kingdom
The king's homage and Daniel's promotion

doctrines.note: The stone that becomes a mountain is a kingdom set up by God himself, not built by human hands, which outlasts and replaces every empire. This is the book's first statement of the kingdom of God that Jesus would later announce.
What human wisdom cannot reach, God reveals. Daniel's knowledge comes not from technique but from the God who "reveals the deep and hidden things" (verse 22).
God "removes kings and establishes them" (verse 21). Even the head of gold received his power from the God of heaven (verse 37), and that power is on loan.
Faced with death, Daniel gathers his friends to plead for mercy, and when the answer comes he stops to bless God before running to the king. Petition and thanksgiving frame the revelation.

words.note: Raz, mystery or secret, probably a loanword from Persian. It refers to something hidden that only God can reveal. The Dead Sea Scrolls use it for God's hidden purposes, and the New Testament's Greek word for mystery carries the same sense: a secret plan of God now made known.

Peshar, interpretation, used again and again in this chapter. The related Hebrew word gives its name to the pesharim, Dead Sea Scroll commentaries that interpret prophetic texts as referring to the community's own day. In Daniel the interpretation belongs to God as much as the dream does.

Malkhu, kingdom, kingship, or reign. The chapter lays the kingdoms of the statue alongside the kingdom God sets up, using the same word for both, to show that God's rule is a real kingdom that competes with and outlasts the others.

Even, stone. The stone is cut out without human hands, a phrase that marks it as God's work. Other biblical passages speak of a stone God lays (Isaiah 28:16) and a rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22), and the New Testament gathers these stone texts around Jesus.

christ: The chapter's hope is a kingdom from God that will fill the earth. Jesus began his preaching by announcing that this kingdom was near (Mark 1:15). He also appears to draw on the image of the crushing stone: after quoting Psalm 118 about the stone the builders rejected, he adds, "Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed" (Luke 20:18), which many interpreters hear as an echo of Daniel 2:34-35, 44-45. The New Testament sees the kingdom as begun in Jesus' ministry, death, and resurrection and completed at his return, when "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ" (Revelation 11:15). The small stone that becomes a mountain also fits Jesus' parables of the kingdom that starts small and grows.

hard.q: Which four kingdoms does the statue represent?
hard.a: The head of gold is named: it is Nebuchadnezzar (verse 38). The rest are not named in this chapter. The traditional Christian reading, found in Jerome and held by many today, takes them as Media-Persia (silver), Greece (bronze), and Rome (iron), with the stone as the kingdom of God coming in Christ during the Roman period. Most critical scholars, and some others, read them as Media, Persia, and Greece, with the mixed iron and clay as the divided Greek kingdoms of the Ptolemies and Seleucids, whose attempts to unite through royal marriages failed (compare verse 43 with 11:6, 17). Supporters of that view note that Daniel treats the Medes as a kingdom before Persia (5:31; 6:28), while supporters of the first view note that 8:20 joins Media and Persia in a single ram. Some futurist readers add that the iron kingdom extends into a revived form at the end of history. All agree on the point the chapter makes most plainly: every human kingdom is temporary, and God's kingdom will replace them all.

questions: Daniel's first response to a death sentence was to ask for time and gather friends to pray. What would that response look like in a crisis you face?
The statue's metals decline in value from gold to clay. What does the dream suggest about how God sees the empires people admire most?
Daniel told the king plainly that the wisdom was not his own. How do you receive credit for gifts that you did not create?
